t.7.6.1: Being oppressed by them, the gods and the sages rich in austerity, stricken with fear, went for refuge to Maheśvara, the god of gods.
t.7.6.2: Having approached the three-eyed one, the foe of Kāma and the foe of Tripura, the gods, with joined palms and speaking in voices stammering with fear, said to him:
t.7.6.3: O Lord, O ruler of creatures, O tormentor of foes, all creatures are being oppressed by the sons of Sukeśa, who have grown arrogant through the boon of the Grandsire.
t.7.6.4: Our hermitages, once places of refuge, have been made places without refuge; Śakra has been driven down from heaven, and in heaven they now sport like Śakra.
t.7.6.5: I am Viṣṇu, I am Rudra, I am Brahmā, I am the king of the gods; I am Yama, I am Varuṇa, I am Candra, and I am also Ravi.
t.7.6.6: Thus, O god, those Rākṣasas, made arrogant by the granting of boons and fierce in battle, torment us, and so do those who march at their head.
t.7.6.7: Therefore, O god, you ought to grant freedom from fear to us who are stricken with fear; assuming a dreadful form, slay these thorns in the side of the gods.
t.7.6.8: Thus addressed by all the gods, the lord Kapardin, the blue-red Nīlalohita, mindful of his regard for Sukeśa, spoke to the hosts of gods.
t.7.6.9: I shall not slay them, for those Asuras cannot be slain by me; but I shall give you counsel concerning the one who will surely slay them.
t.7.6.11: Then they, tormented by fear of the night-rangers, honoured Maheśvara with cries of victory and came into the presence of Viṣṇu.
t.7.6.10: Putting this very undertaking at the forefront, let the bulls among the gods go to Viṣṇu for refuge; that lord will slay them.
t.7.6.12: Having bowed down to the god who bears the conch and the discus, and having honored him greatly, those who were tormented by the sons of Sukeśa spoke these words as if in great agitation.
t.7.6.13: O god, the three sons of Sukeśa, resembling the three sacred fires, have attacked us by the power of the boon granted to them and have seized our abodes.
t.7.6.14: There is a city named Laṅkā, hard to approach, situated on the summit of Trikūṭa. Dwelling there, the night-rangers torment all of us.
t.7.6.15: So you, O Madhusūdana, for our sake, slay them; offer them to Yama, their lotus-faces severed by your discus.
t.7.6.17: Thus addressed by the deities, Janārdana, the god of gods, who brings fear to his enemies, granted them freedom from fear and spoke to the gods.
t.7.6.16: In times of danger there is no one else equal to you who grants us freedom from fear. O god, dispel our fear, as the sun dispels the mist.
t.7.6.18: I know the Rākṣasa Sukeśa, O Īśāna, who has grown proud through the boon granted to him, and I know his sons as well, of whom Mālyavān is the eldest.
t.7.6.19: I shall slay in battle those vilest of rākṣasas who have transgressed all bounds; O gods, be free from your distress.
t.7.6.20: Thus addressed by the mighty Viṣṇu, all those gods, delighted, went each to their own abode, praising Janārdana.
t.7.6.21: Having heard of the preparations of the gods, that night-roaming rākṣasa Mālyavān spoke these words to his two heroic brothers.
t.7.6.22: The immortals and the sages, it is said, having banded together and seeking our destruction, spoke these words to Śaṃkara, the three-eyed one.
t.7.6.23: O god, the sons of Sukeśa, puffed up by the power of the boons granted to them, terrible in form and ever ready for battle, torment us at every step.
t.7.6.24: We have been overpowered by the Rākṣasas, O Umāpati; out of fear of those wicked ones we are not able to remain in our own homes.
t.7.6.25: Therefore, for our welfare, O Three-eyed One, slay those very rākṣasas; burn them with your mere roar of 'huṃ', O best among those who consume with fire.
t.7.6.26: Thus addressed by the thirty gods, the slayer of Andhaka, having listened, shook his head and his hand and spoke these words.
t.7.6.28: He who bears the discus and mace in his hands, Janārdana clad in yellow garments, he will slay them in battle; take refuge in him.
t.7.6.27: O gods, those sons of Sukeśa cannot be slain by me in battle; but I shall give you counsel about the one who will surely slay them.
t.7.6.29: Not having obtained their desire from Hara, they paid homage to the foe of Kāma and went to the abode of Nārāyaṇa, where they related everything to him.
t.7.6.30: Then the gods, headed by Indra, were addressed by Nārāyaṇa: "I shall slay the enemies of the gods; O gods, be free from your distress."
t.7.6.31: O two bulls among the Rākṣasas, Hari has promised the gods, who are stricken with fear, that we shall be slain. Therefore consider what is fitting to be done.
t.7.6.32: It is hard to conquer Nārāyaṇa, who was the death of Hiraṇyakaśipu and of the other enemies of the gods, and who now seeks to kill us.
t.7.6.33: Then Sumālī and Mālī, having heard the words of Mālyavān, spoke to their eldest brother, as Bhaga and Aṃśa would speak to Vāsava.
t.7.6.35: Plunging with floods of weapons into the unshakable ocean of the gods, we have ever conquered the gods in battle; we have no fear caused by death.
t.7.6.34: We have studied well, we have given gifts and gained what we desired, and our sovereignty has been protected. We have attained a life free from sickness, and our own dharma has been firmly established.
t.7.6.36: Nārāyaṇa and Rudra, Śakra and Yama as well, all of them indeed are afraid to stand before us.
t.7.6.38: Therefore today, fully prepared and surrounded by all our forces, let us slay the gods themselves, from whom this danger has arisen.
t.7.6.37: No fault of Viṣṇu is the cause in this matter, O lord of the Rākṣasas; it is through the fault of the gods alone that Viṣṇu's mind has been stirred.
t.7.6.39: Thus Mālī, Sumālī and Mālyavān, the eldest-born and their lord, proclaimed the campaign, and then all those Rākṣasas, enraged, marched out to battle like Jambha, Vṛtra and Bala.
t.7.6.40: With chariots and lordly elephants, and with horses like mountains, with donkeys, with oxen and with camels, with porpoises and with serpents.
t.7.6.41: With makaras, tortoises and fish, with birds equal to Garuḍa, with lions, tigers and boars, and with sṛmaras and yaks as well.
t.7.6.42: Then all the Rākṣasas, proud of their strength and enemies of the gods, will leave Laṅkā and set out for the world of the gods to wage war.
t.7.6.44: Earthly and atmospheric portents alike, fearsome and commanded by Kāla, rose up swiftly for the destruction of the lords of the Rākṣasas.
t.7.6.43: Then the beings who dwelt in Laṅkā, having seen the overthrow of Laṅkā, perceived danger and were utterly dejected on every side.
t.7.6.45: The clouds rain down bones and hot blood as well; the ocean too has overstepped its shore, and the loftiest of mountains are shaking.
t.7.6.46: Letting loose bursts of wild laughter whose sound was like the roar of thunderclouds, spirits by the thousands rushed about on every side, dancing.
t.7.6.47: And a great circle of vultures, with mouths spewing fire, wheels above the Rākṣasas like the wheel of Time.
t.7.6.48: Paying no heed to those great portents, the Rākṣasas, proud of their strength, kept marching on and did not turn back, bound as they were by the noose of Death.
t.7.6.49: Mālyavān, Sumālī and Mālī, the night-roaming rākṣasas, went at their head, as the sacrificial fires go before the sacrifices.
t.7.6.50: And all those night-wanderers took refuge in Mālyavant, who was like the mountain Mālyavant, just as one takes refuge in the Creator of the embodied being.
t.7.6.51: That army of the lords of the Rākṣasas, thundering like great massed clouds and standing under the command of Mālī, marched to the world of the gods out of desire for victory.
t.7.6.52: But the lord Nārāyaṇa, having heard from the messenger of the gods of that mobilization of the Rākṣasas, then set his mind on battle.
t.7.6.53: Hymned by the gods, Siddhas, ṛṣis and great serpents, and sung to by the foremost Gandharvas and the Apsarases, he who bore the discus, the sword, the plough and other excellent weapons advanced upon the army of the enemies of the immortals.
t.7.6.55: Then the night-roaming rākṣasas, in their thousands, surrounded Mādhava and pierced him through with their excellent weapons, sharp and smeared with blood and flesh, their forms like the fire Vaiśvānara at the end of the age.
t.7.6.54: Its flanks driven back by the wind from Suparṇa's wings, its banners whirling and its weapons scattered, that army of the rākṣasa king shook like a dark lord of mountains whose rocks are tumbling loose.
